newsitem.title: USA: Gasoline prices slide as supplies flood market.
newsitem.headline: Gasoline prices slide as supplies flood market.

text.p: Gasoline prices fell again Friday as the market struggled to absorb high imports and record production.

"Demand has been actually very good at around 8.3 million barrels per day (bpd) last week, but record production and high imports combined has just been too much for it," said Tim Evans, an analyst with Pegasus Econometric Research in New York.
Earlier this week, the American Petroleum Institute said gasoline production for the week ended June 13 was a record 8.23 million bpd while imports stood at a hefty 448,000 bpd.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), gasoline for July delivery closed 0.61 cent lower at 55.48 cents a gallon after falling to new life-of-contract low of 55.00 cents.
July crude ended off 12 cents at $18.55 a barrel. July heating oil ended 0.12 cent off at 51.33 cents a gallon.
Some traders noted a general reluctance to take major positions ahead of next week's meeting of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
"It was quite quiet on the news front, but with OPEC coming up no one wanted to take a big position on a Friday night ahead of that kind of meeting," one trader said.
Most market participants believe the 11-nation cartel will "roll over" the current supply quotas and do little to halt the overproduction that has undermined world oil prices.
NYMEX platinum and palladium prices closed higher amid concern about a shortage of both metals with shipments from Russia, a key supplier, still suspended.

Russian exports of platinum group metals (PGM) -- palladium and related metals -- suspended for five months, are due to resume in late June. Russia supplies about 60 percent of the world's palladium and 25 percent of its platinum.
Analysts said even if Russian supplies do resume in late June, the key questions are how much metal the Russians will supply this year and how quickly inventories will be rebuilt.
In early June, Vladimir Rybkin, the director of Gokhran, the precious metals division of Russia's Finance Ministry, said Russia's exports in 1997 would be just slightly lower than 1996 levels.

In 1996, Russia is believed to have run down its stockpiles by exporting 1.22 million ounces of platinum, compared with mine production of only 700,000 ounces, and exporting 4.60 million ounces of palladium, compared with mine production of less than 2.0 million ounces, according to refiners Johnson Matthey.

"But we believe the exporting of only slightly less PGMs in 1997, as compared with 1996 levels, may be a very optimistic goal since Russia would have to export on average nearly double the monthly amount for the remainder of the year compared with the 1996 monthly average," Prudential Securities analyst Clarence Morrison said.

"We believe there is a distinct possibility that much of Russia's above-ground supply has been depleted and the world now has to rely increasingly on mine production, which for Russia may decline in 1997," he said.
NYMEX platinum for July delivery ended up $2.50 at $415.20 an ounce, while NYMEX September palladium gained $2.65 to close at $172.85.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat futures continued to fall, with July delivery slipping to a low of $3.32-1/4 a bushel, the cheapest level for the nearby contract since August 1994. It closed off 2-1/4 cents at $3.34-3/4.

Wheat remained under pressure from active harvesting and reports of better-than-expected yields. Favourable weekend weather should allow harvests to progress rapidly in southern Kansas and in Oklahoma and Texas.
"We have started to hear from our customers that this is one of the best years they've ever seen," said Jason Roose, analyst with U.S. Commodities.
"One (customer) said that one of his wheat areas came in at 76 (bushels per acre). If you continue to see these big numbers, we could drop another 40 cents," he added.
